newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast completes biggest privatisation deal.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast completes biggest privatisation deal.

text.p: Ivory Coast has completed its main privatisation deal by ceding a 51 percent stake in state telephone company CI-TELCOM to France Telecom, which promises investments of more than $450 million over five years.

Industry analysts gave a mixed reaction. Some saw much scope for expansion. Others suggested France Telecom had paid a high price for a heavily indebted company with a payroll of nearly 4,000 and a creaking and dilapidated network.
"It is such an enormous amount of money when you add up what they will pay for the shares and the projected investment," one investment analyst told Reuters.

He said it was difficult to see when to expect returns on such investment given that the Ivory Coast's economy is still heavily dependent on capricious commodity exports, notably cocoa of which it is the world's largest producer.

CI-TELCOM is the crown jewel in Ivory Coast's privatisation programme under which over half of some 60 selected state enterprises ranging from oilpalm estates to banks have been sold off over the past two years.
President Henri Konan Bedie approved the sell-off in a decree on Wednesday.
Ivory Coast and other West African states hope new investment in the privatised telecommunications sector will spur economic growth as it did for the likes of Mexico and Chile.

France Telecom announced on Thursday it plans to invest 250 billion CFA francs ($455 million) over the next five years to expand and modernise the network, creating more than 10,000 direct and indirect jobs in the process.
It said in a statement it plans to provide 300,000 new telephone lines over the same period, more than quadrupling the number of telephones in Ivory Coast.
The Ivorian government announced on Wednesday night, during signing of the accord, that France Telecom would pay 105 billion CFA francs in cash.

France Telecom said in its statement that it had also agreed to pay to the Ivorian state 40 billion CFA of CI-TELCOM's debt, the bulk of which is in fact owed to the French company. It will also recapitalise 51 percent of CI-TELCOM.
Other analysts remained cautiously bullish on the deal, saying there was scope for growth in the sector.

"They are heavily under-invested in the sector. CI-TELCOM is capable of generating growth if it is properly managed, everyone pays their bills and people get phone lines when they request them," a second investment analyst said.

Privatisation of the phone company has generated heated debate in the past month following the disqualification of a bid by local consortium Africa Bell, which was loosely allied with U.S. telecommunications giant AT&T.
Authorities said Africa Bell had not shown enough evidence of financial and technical resources by a set deadline.
The French, bidding through a local consortium including heavyweight Ivorian investors, outbid the only rival, Telekom Malaysia, which had offered 104 billion CFA for the shares.
France Telecom has a long association with Ivory Coast, a former French colony, where the French network is a major supplier, technical partner and creditor.
France Cable Radio, France Telecom's wholly-owned unit through which it bid, includes diversified group SIFCOM, the largest private company in Ivory Coast.
The state plans to retain a 35 percent stake in CI-TELCOM. Eight to 10 percent will be sold to Ivorian shareholders on the Abidjan bourse and staff will be offered one to two percent.
